newsitem.title: UK: Full text of May UK Purchasing Managers' Survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of May UK Purchasing Managers' Survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the May Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply. The survey is sponsored by Reuters.
PMI SIGNALS EXPANSION FOR TWELFTH CONSECUTIVE MONTH AS OUTPUT AND ORDERS SHOW STRONG GROWTH. EXPORT DEMAND REMAINS WEAK.
UK purchasing managers reported the twelfth consecutive monthly expansion in manufacturing activity in May.

The seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers' Index (a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of manufacturing activity) rose to its highest level since April 1995 as manufacturers again increased output to meet substantial growth in orders.

Buoyant domestic demand from consumers continued to boost order books. Thus, despite a further fall in the rate of growth of export orders, attributed to the sustained strength of the pound, UK manufacturers experienced the fastest growth of total orders since last November.

In response to the improved state of order books, manufacturers increased production for the twelfth successive month in May. This in turn provoked further growth in the quantity of goods purchased by manufacturers. The rate of growth of goods purchased dipped slightly, however, and remained subdued relative to output growth, as manufacturers continued to keep stock levels under control for cost considerations.

While the strength of the pound continued to adversely affect UK manufacturing exports, it again reduced the prices of imported materials. A quarter of manufacturers reported a fall in input prices in May compared with one month ago, while only 7.5% reported a rise.

In spite of the increased purchasing activity, the time taken for suppliers to deliver goods to factories lengthened only slightly in May. Suppliers have generally been able to meet manufacturers' rising demand without incurring significant delays. Only 9% of manufacturers reported lengthening lead times in May.

The ability of suppliers to meet existing demand and the continuing trend of low input prices has enabled an increasing number of firms to implement cost-cutting destocking policies. Stocks of purchases fell for the 25th consecutive month.

Growth in the manufacturing workforce continued in May, but remains relatively muted when compared with the accelerating growth of output and orders. The continued need to rationalise production processes to boost efficiencies again prevented any significant overall increase in recruitment.The manufacturing economy expanded for the eleventh consecutive month in April.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

Manufacturing output rose for the twelfth successive month in May, with the seasonally adjusted index recording the highest rate of growth since last September. Firms again increased production to meet further growth in order books. The largest rise was reported in the production of consumer goods, followed by intermediate goods (which rose very sharply in May) and finally investment goods.
NEW ORDERS

The seasonally adjusted New Orders Index registered the fastest rate of growth since last November and the twelfth consecutive monthly improvement in order books. A further strengthening of demand from UK consumers provided the main source of new business. Export orders rose only modestly in the face of the strong pound. The Export Index has fallen sharply since the middle of last year.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The seasonally adjusted Quantity of Purchases Index, at a level well above the 50.0 no change' mark, recorded a further rise in May. Manufacturers continued to increase the quantity of inputs purchased to satisfy greater production requirements. The rate of growth of purchases dipped, however, as many manufacturers continued to keep stock levels under control for cost considerations.
PRICES

The Prices Index signalled a further sharp fall in input prices. A quarter of all manufacturers reported a fall in prices compared with one month ago, while only 7.5% reported a rise. The reduced costs of imports arising from the continued strength of the pound was once more a key factor behind the fall, although the successful negotiation of lower prices with suppliers was again also widely reported.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The seasonally adjusted Suppliers' Delivery Times Index, at a level only marginally less than 50.0, indicated only a very slight lengthening of lead-times in May. This suggests that, despite the current strong growth in demand, suppliers have generally been able to meet orders without incurring significant delays.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

A favourable outlook of continued low prices and good availability of supplies encouraged increasing numbers of firms to implement cost-cutting destocking exercises in May. The Stocks of Purchases Index signalled an acceleration in the rate of decline as a result. Stocks of purchases have now fallen for twenty-five consecutive months.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Stocks of finished goods fell again in May, a fall attributed largely to growth in sales exceeding current rates of production. Following a brief rise in the seasonally adjusted index in April (thought to have been influenced by an increased incidence of stock-building to meet expected growth of demand), the index fell back to a similar level as in March.
EMPLOYMENT

The seasonally adjusted Employment Index rose for the second successive month in May, but continued to register only modest growth in employment. Increased demand for goods was cited as the principal reason for growth in employment, but the continued need to rationalise production processes to boost efficiencies again prevented any significant overall increase in recruitment.
CONSUMER GOODS

The consumer goods industries recorded the highest output index (signalling the greatest monthly rise) of all three sectors in May, and the strongest output growth since last November. Order books also experienced the sharpest improvement of all three sectors. Strong domestic demand from consumers was the principal source of new business while export orders experienced only very moderate growth. The quantity of goods purchased rose sharply and suppliers' delivery times lengthened in May as firms sought to meet increased purchasing requirements. Prices paid for inputs fell sharply, despite the extra demand, again influenced by the strong pound. Employment rose for the second successive month in a muted response to new orders.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

Output and new orders of investment goods experienced similar rates of strong growth in May, albeit slower than recorded in recent months. Growth of export orders for investment goods decelerated but domestic demand remained buoyant. In response to the strength of demand, employment rose in the investment goods industries for the fourth successive month. The quantity of purchases fell very slightly, however, as many firms continued to operate stock reduction policies. Input prices fell sharply for the sixteenth month in succession, influenced not only by lower import prices arising from the exchange rate, but also by the continued ability of firms to negotiate lower prices with certain suppliers operating at below full capacity.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

The intermediate goods industries reported a sharp rise in production in May. The Output Index rose markedly to its highest level since November 1994. This was driven by an acceleration in the growth of new orders from UK markets and a marginal increase in export orders. The rate of growth of the quantity of goods purchased by firms rose for the second month in succession to meet the rising production requirements. Prices of these raw materials fell again in May with the index remaining well below the no change' level of 50.0. Lower import prices, resulting from the strength of the pound, again helped to keep prices down. The Employment Index for intermediate goods industries registered a return to growth following two months of decline.
